name: Gloria Macapagal Arroyo
role: President of the Philippines (2001-2010); later House Speaker (2018-2019)
summary: Philippine president who combined market-oriented economic management with anti-poverty programmes, a close US alliance and Catholic-aligned social policy. She signed abolition of the death penalty, anti-terror surveillance and agrarian-reform laws, and later pushed charter change toward federalism.

death-penalty.rationale: She signed the 2006 law abolishing the death penalty (RA 9346) and, as Deputy Speaker, voted no on its reinstatement in the House in 2017.

surveillance-ok.rationale: She signed the Human Security Act, whose Section 7 authorises police surveillance and interception of terrorism suspects on a written Court of Appeals order and excludes lawyer-client and similar communications.

land-redistribution.rationale: She signed RA 9700, which limits acquisition after June 2009 to voluntary offers and compulsory acquisition of agricultural lands above 50 hectares.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: She signed the Magna Carta of Women, whose Section 38 renames the national women's commission the Philippine Commission on Women as the primary body on gender equality.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: The Magna Carta of Women she signed sets a 50-50 gender balance goal in third-level civil service posts and at least 40 percent women on development councils.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The Magna Carta of Women she signed guarantees women equal rights to the use and management of land, and RA 9700 extends support services equally to women and men beneficiaries.

free-trade.rationale: At the UN in 2007 she said the global trading system alleviates poverty through market forces and that the country cannot afford to fear globalization, while saying it is not ready to compete everywhere.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: She asked developed countries to open markets, end heavy farm subsidies and make the Doha round a true development round (2001, 2007).

priority-to-poor.rationale: She told the UN in 2007 that poverty alleviation is the most important part of her agenda and the country's number-one issue.

limit-growth.rationale: She rejected the view that the environment must be sacrificed to growth and said the country would grow its economy and sustain nature together.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: She said overdependence on external markets is a peril and expanding domestic demand is largely each nation's responsibility (2001), and presented self-reliance in food and energy as the Philippine approach (2008).

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: She said political autonomy must be made accessible to regions that want it, within the sovereignty of the nation, as part of the approach to Muslim and tribal minorities.

right-to-secede.rationale: She contrasted negotiating with secessionist groups with 'dismembering our country' and tied autonomy to remaining within national sovereignty.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: She called the United States the country's strongest strategic ally and said she expected to keep building the alliance.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: She called on Myanmar to return to democracy, release Aung San Suu Kyi and involve the opposition in its constitutional process.

universal-healthcare.rationale: She reported expanding PhilHealth insurance to 86 percent of the population by 2009, including subsidised cover for the poorest, and promised to fund premiums of the poorest from sin taxes.

public-ownership.rationale: She signed the Electric Power Industry Reform Act, which provides for privatising the generation assets of the National Power Corporation.

legalize-drugs.rationale: She signed the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act, which penalises use of dangerous drugs (Section 15, mandatory rehabilitation for a first offence) as well as trafficking.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: She reported titling Certificates of Ancestral Domain over 525,000 hectares and 700,000 indigenous owners of their land under her administration.

limit-population.rationale: She credited promoting natural family planning and female education with curbing population growth to 2.04 percent and urged informing couples about natural methods.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Under her Proclamation 1017 of 2006 the government cancelled rally permits, made warrantless arrests of opposition figures and raided a newspaper; the Court later held several of these acts unlawful and voided her power to issue decrees.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: In 2024 she voted no on the absolute divorce bill, whose grounds include a five-year separation without fault.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: She chose scholarships at private high schools over building more public ones (2007) and reported government financing half of private high school students (2009).

social-market-economy.rationale: In 2009 she said the market grows economies, 'a free market, not a free-for-all', and in 2007 she set out a stronger and wider social safety net as a funding priority.

rich-first.rationale: She presented the Super Regions plan as a way to spread development away from an inequitable concentration in Metro Manila.

rent-control.rationale: In her 2009 address she reported the rent control law capping annual rent increases at 10 percent in 2005-2008 and at 7 percent after a moratorium under the law she had just signed.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: She signed RA 9851, which applies equally to heads of state and government and lets Philippine authorities surrender suspects to the appropriate international court.

government-encourage-intercultural-conta.rationale: She described a Philippine model of reconciliation built on inter-faith dialogue and expanded public works for Mindanao, and pledged interfaith dialogue meetings (2007, 2008).

allow-dual-citizenship.rationale: She signed RA 9225, under which natural-born Filipinos who took foreign citizenship re-acquire or retain Philippine citizenship.

torture-always-illegal.rationale: She signed the Anti-Torture Act, which says war, internal political instability or any other public emergency can never justify torture.

notes: Themes searched: economy (VAT, EPIRA privatisation, agrarian reform, rent control, health insurance, medicines law), government (EO 464, Proclamation 1017, charter change, term extension), liberty (death penalty, drug law, torture, surveillance, divorce), society and women's rights, world (UN speeches 2001-2008, Iraq withdrawal, US alliance, international criminal law), ecology, and her State of the Nation addresses of 2007-2009. Her family-planning and reproductive-health stance was recorded only through secondhand reports of a bill whose clauses do not settle abortion or sex education, so those stay null. The Official Gazette copies of her 2001-2006 State of the Nation addresses could not be downloaded by any agent, so those are not used. The record is thin on ethnonationalism, nationalism, secularism, class conflict and the pluralism/authoritarianism line, so the uncertainty rule is not met.
